contributions: an explicit diagnosis of two distinct failure modes of uniform length-penalty RL: sequence-level over-compression of critical early reasoning tokens, and group-level indiscriminate compression that ignores query difficulty

prefix-protected optimization, anchoring early reasoning in a frozen reference policy's valid solution path via a linearly-decaying hybrid rollout distribution, preventing premature reasoning collapse from over-compressing the logical foundation
a difficulty-aware penalty that scales length-penalty strength by each query's empirically-measured pass rate, relaxing constraints on hard queries while strictly enforcing conciseness on easy ones

the only method among nine training-free and training-based baselines to simultaneously exceed 45% token reduction and improve accuracy over the vanilla model, with demonstrated generalization across model scales, out-of-domain tasks (science, code, instruction-following), and alternative length-reward formulations (cosine reward)

a behavioral analysis (Advance/Reflect/Refine/Verify categorization) showing the compression specifically suppresses redundant self-correction and hesitation rather than constructive reasoning content
limitations: The paper does not discuss limitations explicitly in the excerpted sections; the difficulty-aware penalty relies on empirical pass rate from sampled prefix rollouts as a difficulty proxy, which requires additional group sampling during training (computational overhead versus a simpler uniform penalty is not directly quantified in the excerpted material); the prefix-protection mechanism requires a hyperparameter search over initial prefix length and decay duration K, shown to be sensitive (both too-short and too-long prefixes underperform the tuned setting).
method: PACE combines two mechanisms within GRPO. Sequence level (prefix-protected optimization): for each training query, rejection sampling from a frozen initial (reference) policy selects the shortest correct sample as a fixed reasoning prefix (or the shortest sample overall if none is correct); early in training, the rollout distribution is a hybrid that strictly follows this frozen prefix policy up to a prefix length S(k) and then switches to the current training policy for the remainder, anchoring the reasoning path in a valid logical foundation before compression pressure applies; S(k) linearly decays from an initial length L_init to zero over K training steps, so the safeguard is gradually removed as training progresses, letting the policy eventually generate the full sequence unconstrained. Group level (difficulty-aware penalty): quantifies each query's difficulty via the empirical pass rate rho(q) over a sampled group of prefix rollouts (lower pass rate = harder); scales the length-penalty strength via alpha(rho) = 1 - cos(pi/2 * rho), which approaches its maximum (strict length penalty) as rho -> 1 (easy queries) and decays toward zero as rho -> 0 (hard queries), so difficult problems retain their needed exploration/reasoning budget while easy problems are strictly compressed. The two mechanisms combine into one GRPO-compatible reward and advantage computation, with importance-sampling correction (since prefix-anchored rollouts are off-policy relative to the pure current policy) and a KL penalty against the reference policy under the hybrid prefix distribution.
methods: PACE (Prefix-protected and difficulty-Aware Compression for Efficient reasoning)
one_liner: PACE identifies two distinct failure modes of uniform length-penalty RL for efficient reasoning -- sequence-level over-compression of critical early deduction steps, and group-level indiscriminate compression that ignores query difficulty -- and fixes both with a frozen-policy prefix-rollout anchor (decaying over training) plus a pass-rate-derived, difficulty-scaled length penalty, becoming the only compared method to cut token usage over 45% while simultaneously improving accuracy, and generalizing to code, science and instruction-following domains.
problem: Length-penalty RL for LRM overthinking applies a uniform penalty to every token and every query, which causes two distinct failure modes: at the sequence level, compressing the earliest reasoning tokens (which serve as the logical anchor for the whole derivation) causes the model to skip essential deduction steps and produce shortcut/incorrect answers; at the group level, applying the same length constraint regardless of query difficulty disproportionately shortens reasoning on hard problems (where accuracy degrades sharply as training progresses) while under-penalizing easy ones.

relevance.overthinking: Directly and centrally relevant: it names overthinking explicitly and provides a precise, mechanistic diagnosis of exactly why naive length-penalty RL for overthinking mitigation fails in two distinct, separable ways (destroying the logical anchor at the start of a trace; ignoring that harder problems genuinely need more reasoning budget) -- both of which are load-bearing assumptions in many other length-penalty methods in this archive that this paper's ablations show are necessary to address explicitly rather than assume away, and its behavioral (Advance/Reflect/Refine/Verify) decomposition gives a concrete, checkable way to distinguish genuine compression of redundant hesitation from harmful compression of constructive reasoning.

results: Across four in-domain math benchmarks (AIME24/25, MATH500, GSM8K) on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B/1.5B, PACE is the only method (among ThinkSwitcher, DEER, Dynasor-CoT, O1-Pruner, DAST, AdaptThink, DR.SAF, Efficient-R baselines) that achieves both >45% token reduction and an accuracy *improvement* over the vanilla model simultaneously: on the 7B model, 54.8% average token reduction with accuracy 69.5% (vs. vanilla's 68.9%, +0.6); on the 1.5B model, 46.6% token reduction with accuracy 57.3% (vs. vanilla's 53.2%, +4.1) -- nearly double the token-reduction rate of the second-best performer (AdaptThink, 28.5% TR on 7B) while also exceeding its accuracy. Aggressive training-free pruners (DR.SAF, DEER) achieve high token-reduction rates but at accuracy cost (DR.SAF -2.7pp, DEER -2.3pp on 7B), while conservative methods (AdaptThink) preserve accuracy but yield much smaller efficiency gains -- PACE dominates the Pareto frontier rather than trading off along it. Out-of-domain generalization (trained exclusively on math data) extends to GPQA-Diamond (science), LiveCodeBench-v6 (code), and IF-Eval (instruction-following): the 1.5B model shows 1.1-4.6% accuracy improvements with 14.5-37.0% token reduction across these domains; the 7B model achieves up to 1.8% accuracy gain with 25.7-33.3% token reduction -- both accuracy and efficiency gains transfer beyond the mathematical training domain. Ablations (7B model) confirm both mechanisms are necessary: removing group-level (difficulty-aware) control causes a significant performance drop (-9.8pp on AIME24, -12.9pp on MATH500), attributed to indiscriminate compression causing 'reasoning collapse' during training (training accuracy and entropy both destabilize/oscillate, per Figure 3); removing sequence-level (prefix) control also degrades performance sharply since compression then starts from the initial tokens, causing the model to skip essential reasoning steps. A prefix-length sweep on the 7B model shows even a modest prefix (256 tokens) improves accuracy over no prefix (90.2%->92.0%), peaking at 512 tokens (93.1%), but an excessively long prefix (1024 tokens) harms performance (90.3%) because the model comes to fully rely on the frozen prefix, exposing the ground-truth path too early during initial training and inducing 'shortcut learning' that degrades reasoning capability once the prefix protection is removed. Behavioral analysis (annotating generated CoT into Advance/Reflect/Refine/Verify categories via Qwen3-32B) across training shows the proportion of 'Advance' (forward-progressing) steps rises from 61.5% to 72.5% while 'Reflect' and 'Verify' steps decline (18.5%->13.6%, 14.0%->9.8% respectively) -- direct evidence that PACE's token reduction comes from suppressing redundant self-correction and excessive hesitation rather than omitting constructive logical content. A per-difficulty-level breakdown on MATH500 (5 levels) shows a 'No Control' (uniform penalty) ablation suffers catastrophic accuracy collapse on hard problems (Level 1: 0.96 -> Level 5: 0.07), while PACE's accuracy stays comparable to the unconstrained original model across all difficulty levels, even slightly exceeding it at Level 4 (0.79 vs. 0.77) at 58% shorter length -- evidence that targeted compression can reduce redundant reasoning noise on complex problems, not just preserve accuracy. Testing generalization to an alternative length-reward formulation (a static cosine reward penalizing length by z-score) shows the baseline cosine-reward-only training suffers catastrophic training-accuracy collapse after ~150 steps, while combining PACE's dual-level control with the same cosine reward avoids this collapse and achieves consistently better accuracy-length trade-offs across AIME24/25/MATH500 -- confirming PACE's mechanisms generalize across different underlying length-penalty reward designs, not just its own default one.
